title: Why Maritime Decarbonisation is the Caribbean’s…
summary: The Caribbean's heavy reliance on maritime shipping for 80-90% of food imports and significant cruise traffic exposes the region's vulnerability to dirty shipping practices and impending decarbonization costs. While the IMO's 2023 GHG Strategy sets ambitious 2050 targets, the critical focus must be on immediate short and mid-term measures to curb excessive emissions, not just distant promises. Without robust technical regulations and fair carbon pricing, vulnerable nations risk bearing the financial burden of a sector historically slow to transition from high-carbon HFO.
content:
The global maritime sector is undergoing an environmental overhaul that is driven by an urgent

mandate to eliminate its carbon footprint. For the Caribbean, this is an existential reality and not

merely an abstract policy discussion happening on distant shores. As Small Island Developing

States, the Caribbean’s relationship with the sea is two-fold as it is on the front lines of climate

change, yet completely reliant on marine transport to sustain daily life.

Maritime shipping serves as the heartbeat of Caribbean economies, delivering between 80%

and 90% of all imported food consumed in the region, while sharing its waters with a tourism

sector that commands roughly 43% of global cruise traffic. Decarbonizing this sector therefore,

is a high-stakes balancing act. If done poorly, new international regulations could drive up

freight costs and severely threaten regional food security. If executed equitably, however, it

offers a generational opportunity for the Caribbean to transition away from imported fossil fuels

and catalyze a resilient green economy.

The global framework for this transformation was solidified when the International Maritime

Organization (IMO) adopted its historic 2023 GHG Strategy. This milestone agreement set

highly ambitious targets, aiming to slash greenhouse gas emissions and reach a net-zero

trajectory for international shipping by or around 2050. However, the true test of this strategy

lies in the ongoing negotiation and adoption of subsequent short and mid-term measures.

These technical regulations and economic mechanisms, such as global fuel standards and

maritime carbon pricing systems, will dictate the immediate financial realities of global trade. For

vulnerable island economies like ours, participating in the design of these near-term measures

is vital. Without a strong and unified regional voice, these impending emission penalties could

unfairly penalize the region’s import-dependent nations before they have the infrastructure to

adapt.

Historically, the Caribbean faced a severe capacity deficit at this specialized intersection of

climate science, maritime law, and economic policy. This gap became increasingly visible during

the Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) 80 negotiations where key

decarbonization frameworks were finalized, and seeing only four out of sixteen Caribbean IMO

member states represented.

To reverse this trend and secure a fair transition, regional stakeholders mobilized, culminating in

the August 2024 launch of the University of the West Indies Caribbean Shipping Lanes Project

(UWI-CSL). Housed at the Shridath Ramphal Centre (SRC), UWI-CSL was designed to address

these deficiencies.

By focusing on technical advisory work, delegate training, and regional coordination, UWI-CSL

has quickly built up the Caribbean’s diplomatic muscle, especially at the IMO. The project has

already facilitated national consultations across several countries and successfully delivered the

first-ever joint Caribbean submission to the IMO. Through the evidence-based support of UWI-

CSL, regional leaders are no longer passive bystanders , as they are now actively shaping

global maritime policy to ensure the green transition is both impactful and equitable for the

Caribbean.

Submitted by the UWI-Caribbean Shipping Lanes Project (UWI-CSL)
